chunks.heading: What are related rates?
chunks.body: Sometimes two changing quantities are linked, so as one grows, the other must grow too. Their speeds of change are called related rates.
chunks.checkText: Related rates describes a situation where...

checkOptions.text: Two changing quantities are linked, so their rates of change are connected
Two quantities always change at exactly the same speed
A single rate that never changes over time

chunks.heading: Why the rates connect
chunks.body: Picture a splash of paint spreading in a circle. Its area depends on its radius, and its radius depends on time — so area depends on time too, through the radius.
chunks.checkText: In the spreading paint splash, why does the area change over time?

checkOptions.text: Because the area depends on the radius, which itself changes over time
Because area and radius have no connection to each other
Because time depends on the area

chunks.heading: Chaining the two rates together
chunks.body: Because area and radius are [[mathext1-related-rates-shared-variable|linked]], the chain rule connects their rates: dA/dt equals dA/dr times dr/dt. This turns an unknown rate into a known one.
chunks.checkText: The chain rule dA/dt = dA/dr × dr/dt lets you...

checkOptions.text: Turn an unknown rate into one built from known rates
Prove that two different rates are always equal
Cancel the radius out of the problem entirely

chunks.heading: The two-step method
chunks.body: First, write one quantity as a function of the other, like area in terms of radius. Then differentiate both sides with respect to time using the [[mathext1-related-rates-chain-rule|chain rule]].
chunks.checkText: The first step in a related rates problem is to...

checkOptions.text: Write one quantity as a function of the other
Immediately substitute in the given numbers
Find the second derivative of the function

chunks.heading: Worked example: the paint splash
chunks.body: If area A = πr², then dA/dt = 2πr × dr/dt. When r = 3 cm and dr/dt = 4 cm/s, dA/dt = 2π(3)(4) ≈ 75 cm²/s.
chunks.checkText: In this worked example, what does dA/dt ≈ 75 cm²/s represent?

checkOptions.text: The rate the splash's area is growing at that instant
The splash's radius in centimetres
The total area of the splash so far

chunks.heading: Keep the units straight
chunks.body: Always check units match before substituting, like centimetres with centimetres, not centimetres with metres. A related rates answer is meaningless without the right units attached.
chunks.checkText: Before substituting values into a related rates equation, you should always...

checkOptions.text: Check that all the units match
Convert every value into a percentage
Ignore units until the very end

chunks.heading: What is a differential equation?
chunks.body: A differential equation is an equation containing a derivative. Instead of solving for a number, you solve for the function itself.
chunks.checkText: Solving a differential equation means finding...

checkOptions.text: A function
A single number
The units of a derivative

chunks.heading: The natural growth equation
chunks.body: Natural growth happens when a quantity's rate of change is proportional to the quantity itself. This is written as the [[mathext1-diff-equation-meaning|differential equation]] dQ/dt = kQ.
chunks.checkText: In the equation dQ/dt = kQ, the rate of change of Q is proportional to...

checkOptions.text: Q itself
Time only, not Q
A fixed constant with no link to Q

chunks.heading: Solving dQ/dt = kQ
chunks.body: The function that solves [[mathext1-exp-growth-equation|dQ/dt = kQ]] is Q = Ae^(kt), where A and k are constants. This exponential shape is the only one that works.
chunks.checkText: The solution to the differential equation dQ/dt = kQ has the form...

checkOptions.text: Q = Ae^(kt)
Q = kt + A
Q = A divided by kt

chunks.heading: What A means: the starting value
chunks.body: In [[mathext1-exp-growth-solution|Q = Ae^(kt)]], putting t = 0 gives Q = A. So A is just the value of Q at the very start, often written Q0.
chunks.checkText: In Q = Ae^(kt), the constant A represents...

checkOptions.text: The value of Q when t = 0
The rate of change of Q
The final value Q eventually reaches

chunks.heading: What k means: the growth constant
chunks.body: In [[mathext1-exp-growth-solution|Q = Ae^(kt)]], k is called the growth constant. A bigger k makes the quantity grow faster.
chunks.checkText: The constant k in Q = Ae^(kt) is called the...

checkOptions.text: Growth constant
Initial value
Time constant

chunks.heading: When k is negative: decay
chunks.body: If [[mathext1-growth-constant-k|k]] is negative, the quantity shrinks towards zero instead of growing. This is exponential decay, often written Q = Ae^(−kt) with k now positive.
chunks.checkText: Exponential decay happens when the growth constant is...

checkOptions.text: Negative
Positive
Exactly zero

chunks.heading: k isn't the same as percentage growth
chunks.body: The [[mathext1-growth-constant-k|growth constant]] k is not the ordinary percentage growth rate per year. It measures instantaneous change, which is always a bit different from the average change over a year.
chunks.checkText: The growth constant k is best described as...

checkOptions.text: An instantaneous rate, not the average yearly percentage growth
Exactly equal to the yearly percentage growth
A number with no real meaning

chunks.heading: A new pattern: rate depends on a gap
chunks.body: Sometimes the rate of change is proportional not to Q itself, as in [[mathext1-exp-growth-equation|natural growth]], but to the gap between Q and some fixed value B: dQ/dt = k(Q − B).
chunks.checkText: In dQ/dt = k(Q − B), the rate of change is proportional to...

checkOptions.text: The difference between Q and the fixed value B
Q alone
B alone

chunks.heading: Solving dQ/dt = k(Q − B)
chunks.body: The solution to [[mathext1-modified-growth-equation|dQ/dt = k(Q − B)]] is Q = B + Ae^(kt). It looks like ordinary growth, just shifted up by B.
chunks.checkText: The solution to dQ/dt = k(Q − B) is...

checkOptions.text: Q = B + Ae^(kt)
Q = B × Ae^(kt)
Q = Ae^(kt) − B

chunks.heading: Where the quantity settles
chunks.body: When k is negative in [[mathext1-modified-growth-solution|Q = B + Ae^(kt)]], the Ae^(kt) part shrinks to zero over time. So Q settles down towards B.
chunks.checkText: If k is negative in Q = B + Ae^(kt), as time passes Q gets closer to...

checkOptions.text: B
A
Zero

chunks.heading: Newton's law of cooling
chunks.body: A hot object cools at a rate proportional to the gap between its temperature and the surrounding air, matching the [[mathext1-modified-growth-equation|modified growth pattern]]. The same law also describes a cold object warming up.
chunks.checkText: Newton's law of cooling says the cooling rate is proportional to...

checkOptions.text: The difference between the object's temperature and the surrounding temperature
The object's temperature alone
The amount of time elapsed alone
